title: Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. (Apr 2013 TCC) Case
subject: Conditionally Repayable Contributions as Government Assistance (Tax Court)
summary: Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 103, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision holding that $3,786,474 in conditionally repayable Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency contributions were "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. For Canadian claimants, such funding reduces SR&ED expenditure pools and qualified expenditures, eliminating the related refundable investment tax credits claimed.
metaDescription: Review the April 2013 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. regarding Canadian R&D tax claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
1.1 Overview of the Litigation and Procedural History

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2013 TCC 103 (Docket 2011-245(IT)G), delivered on April 10, 2013 by the Honourable Justice Lucie Lamarre, stands as a foundational authority in Canadian tax jurisprudence governing the interaction between public-sector innovation funding and Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The ruling directly addresses whether conditionally repayable financial contributions disbursed by a federal regional development agency constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"), thereby reducing a taxpayer's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) and its "qualified expenditures" eligible for Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under subsection 127(18).

The litigation originated from Notices of Determination issued by the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") pursuant to paragraph 152(1)(b) of the ITA, dated March 14, 2008 for the 2005 and 2006 taxation years and July 15, 2009 for the 2007 and 2008 taxation years, across four consecutive taxation years (ended March 31, 2005 through March 31, 2008): 2005, 2006, 2007, and 2008. Following Justice Lamarre's dismissal of the taxpayer's appeal in the Tax Court of Canada on April 10, 2013, the taxpayer appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal. On September 11, 2014, a unanimous panel of the Federal Court of Appeal (Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196, Docket A-171-13, per Boivin J.A., Nadon and Trudel JJ.A. concurring) upheld Justice Lamarre's decision in its entirety. The taxpayer subsequently sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada (Docket 36177), which dismissed the application with costs on March 26, 2015, cementing the Tax Court's analytical framework as settled law across Canada.

body.text: 1.2 The Taxpayer's Claim and Commercial Context

The appellant, Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. ("Immunovaccine"), is a Canadian biotechnology company headquartered in Halifax, Nova Scotia, engaged in scientific research and experimental development to create novel vaccine delivery platforms and vaccines targeting infectious diseases and oncology indications. Given the capital-intensive nature of pre-clinical and clinical vaccine development, Immunovaccine sought external financing to support its multi-year research operations in Atlantic Canada.

On December 31, 2004, Immunovaccine entered into a formal contribution agreement (the "Agreement") with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency ("ACOA"), a federal Crown agency mandated to foster economic development and technological innovation in Canada's Atlantic provinces. Under the Agreement, ACOA agreed to provide nearly $3.8 million in financial contributions to defray specified costs of Immunovaccine's research and development activities across the 2005, 2006, 2007, and 2008 taxation years. Over that four-year span, Immunovaccine received a cumulative total of $3,786,474 from ACOA.

In computing its corporate income tax liability and filing its SR&ED claims (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31) for the 2005 through 2008 taxation years, Immunovaccine took the position that the $3,786,474 received under the ACOA Agreement constituted an ordinary commercial loan rather than a grant, subsidy, or "forgivable loan". Because the Agreement contained repayment mechanics tied to future gross revenues, the taxpayer asserted that the inflows were bona fide debt obligations falling outside the statutory definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Consequently, Immunovaccine did not deduct the $3,786,474 from its cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) or from its annual "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(18), claiming full entitlement to Refundable Investment Tax Credits ("RITCs") pursuant to subsection 127.1(1).
1.3 The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon auditing Immunovaccine's SR&ED claims for the 2005, 2006, 2007, and 2008 taxation years, the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA"), acting on behalf of the Minister, examined the substantive terms of the December 31, 2004 ACOA Agreement. By determinations dated March 14, 2008 (for the 2005 and 2006 taxation years) and July 15, 2009 (for the 2007 and 2008 taxation years), the Minister issued Notices of Determination pursuant to paragraph 152(1)(b) of the ITA, ruling that the $3,786,474 disbursed by ACOA constituted "government assistance" within the meaning of subsection 127(9).

The Minister's position rested on the principle that the SR&ED tax incentive regime is designed to subsidize only the net, out-of-pocket costs borne by a taxpayer in performing research and development in Canada. By classifying the ACOA disbursements as government assistance received in respect of SR&ED, the Minister reduced Immunovaccine's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) and reduced its qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar under subsection 127(18), resulting in the complete disallowance of the associated SR&ED expenditure claims and the denial of RITCs under subsection 127.1(1) for each of the four taxation years.
1.4 Governing Statutory Framework in Canada

The dispute in Immunovaccine operates within a tightly integrated statutory architecture in the ITA designed to prevent "double-dipping"—the simultaneous receipt of direct public grants or non-commercial subsidies and federal SR&ED investment tax credits on the exact same dollar of research expenditure. The first pillar of this architecture is the SR&ED expenditure pool governed by subsection 37(1). Under paragraph 37(1)(a) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may deduct current expenditures of a scientific research and experimental development nature directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer via a cumulative expenditure pool. However, paragraph 37(1)(d) mandates that this deductible pool be reduced by all amounts of "government assistance" or "non-government assistance" (as defined in subsection 127(9)) in respect of SR&ED that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing-due date of the income tax return for the year. Conversely, if the taxpayer subsequently repays an amount of assistance that previously reduced the pool under paragraph 37(1)(d), paragraph 37(1)(c) permits the repaid amount to be added back to the SR&ED deductible pool in the taxation year of actual repayment.

The second statutory pillar governs the reduction of qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsections 127(9) and 127(18). Investment Tax Credits under subsection 127(5) and Refundable Investment Tax Credits for Canadian-controlled private corporations ("CCPCs") under subsection 127.1(1) are calculated as a specified percentage of a taxpayer's "qualified expenditures" incurred in the year. Subsection 127(18) explicitly dictates that where a person or partnership has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive government assistance, non-government assistance, or a contract payment in respect of an SR&ED project on or before the filing-due date for a taxation year, the taxpayer's qualified expenditures are reduced by the amount of that assistance. Under paragraphs (e.1) and (e.2) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), coupled with subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8), any subsequent repayment of government assistance generates an ITC addition only in the taxation year in which the repayment actually occurs.

The third pillar—and the precise fulcrum of the Immunovaccine litigation—is the statutory definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, which, as it read for the taxation years at issue, defined the term as "assistance from a government, municipality or other public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance or as any other form of assistance", excluding only assistance in the form of a deduction under subsection 127(5) or 127(6). Finally, the fourth statutory pillar addresses income inclusion for unapplied inducements or assistance under paragraph 12(1)(x). Where government assistance is received by a taxpayer in the course of earning income from a business or property and does not otherwise reduce the capital cost of property or deductible expenditure pools—such as where assistance exceeds the available SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(d)—subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) requires the excess assistance to be included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income in the year of receipt.
1.5 The Court's Final Holding

Justice Lamarre dismissed Immunovaccine's appeals and confirmed the Minister's determinations for the 2005, 2006, 2007, and 2008 taxation years, with costs to the respondent. The Tax Court held that the statutory phrase "or as any other form of assistance" in subsection 127(9) must be given a broad, purposive interpretation rather than being artificially restricted to unilateral grants or traditional forgivable loans. Applying the established commerciality test from Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc., [1996] 3 C.T.C. 246, 96 D.T.C. 6527 (FCA) and The Queen v. Consumers' Gas Company Ltd., [1987] 2 F.C. 60, 87 D.T.C. 5008 (FCA), Justice Lamarre evaluated whether ACOA advanced the funds in the manner of a private commercial lender seeking a business return or as a public authority executing a governance mandate.

Because ACOA acted pursuant to its statutory mandate under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act, carrying out a legislative scheme (the Atlantic Innovation Fund) of distributing funds to encourage those engaged in business to embark on certain classes of enterprise, and provided $3,786,474 on non-commercial terms—characterized by zero interest (interest being chargeable only on overpayments, defaults or overdue amounts), repayment only to the extent the taxpayer earned gross revenues from any source (at 2% of Gross Revenues below $5,000,000 and 10% at or above $5,000,000, with the first instalment due only on December 1, 2008), a maximum recovery capped at the amount of the contribution so that ACOA could never earn a net profit, and obligations to perform the work and exploit the resulting products in Atlantic Canada—the Court held that the contributions were not ordinary commercial loans. The Court further found that Article 6 of the Agreement ("Other Government Assistance"), read together with section 7.1 of Schedule 2, showed that both parties considered the contribution to be government assistance; on appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal additionally observed that the Agreement ends in 2017 whether or not there has been repayment (2014 FCA 196, para. 16). They constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), mandating the reduction of Immunovaccine's SR&ED expenditure pools and eliminating its claimed RITCs under subsection 127.1(1).
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of Immunovaccine's SR&ED tax credit claims stemmed from a single legal determination—that the ACOA contribution was "government assistance" under subsection 127(9)—and the analysis below examines four interconnected legal, contractual, and structural dimensions of that outcome. Rather than involving a dispute over the underlying scientific validity of the vaccine research under subsection 248(1), the failure in Immunovaccine represents a classic funded-research exclusion trap: the taxpayer executed a public funding agreement containing concessional, non-commercial terms and claimed its SR&ED expenditures and RITCs without reducing them for the ACOA contribution, which, once characterized as government assistance, triggered the statutory reduction under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18); the Court's reasons did not address cost segregation, the sole issue before it being the characterization of the contribution.
2.1 Statutory Interpretation Failure: Misapplication of the Ejusdem Generis Canon to Subsection 127(9)

One of Immunovaccine's principal legal arguments—advanced alongside its primary position that the contribution was an ordinary loan advanced on reasonable terms for business purposes—rested on a narrow, formalistic reading of the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA. The taxpayer argued that because Parliament specifically enumerated five categories of assistance—"grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance"—before adding the general phrase "or as any other form of assistance", the Court was bound to apply the ejusdem generis (limited class) rule of statutory interpretation.

Under this interpretive theory, Immunovaccine advanced two distinct legal propositions. First, the taxpayer asserted that the common factor linking the enumerated items is that each represents a transfer of funds advanced with no expectation of repayment, so that the class of items constituting government assistance is limited to non-repayable forms of assistance and closed to any transfer or advance of funds for which repayment is required. Second, the taxpayer argued that the ACOA contribution was not a "forgivable loan" within subsection 127(9), but rather a regular loan, which is not part of that definition. Relying on the definition of a forgivable loan in Interpretation Bulletin IT-340R—a loan made to enable the borrower to pursue an education or carry out a research project and which the lender is committed to forgive if certain conditions are met—Immunovaccine contended that it was required to repay the full amount advanced according to a mandatory repayment schedule out of all of its gross revenues, that no criteria or conditions committed ACOA to forgive the advance, and that section 7.1(b) of Schedule 1 of the Agreement (termination where the Schedule 4 commercialization undertakings have been fulfilled and the taxpayer demonstrates that Gross Revenues have not been or will not continue to be generated) merely reflected the de facto business reality that a loan to an unsuccessful start-up may not be recoverable.

Justice Lamarre (at paragraph 45 of her Reasons for Judgment, later expressly endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal at paragraph 15) dismantled this interpretive artifice. The Court agreed that the enumerated terms in subsection 127(9) appear to be an attempt to describe all possible forms of assistance, and that the inclusion of "forgivable loan" suggests that "government assistance" extends beyond acts of the government which are purely gratuitous; it therefore rejected the proposition that the common factor linking the enumerated terms is a transfer of funds advanced with no expectation of repayment. Crucially, the Court inferred from the statutory context—under which SR&ED deductions and related credits are deferred until the government assistance is actually repaid—Parliament's intention to restrict access to tax relief where relief was provided in some other form, and the Federal Court of Appeal added that the phrase "or as any other form of assistance" does not restrict, but gives a broad meaning to, the word "assistance," capable of encompassing agreements which are not purely gratuitous and unilateral. By relying on a rigid semantic distinction between a "forgivable loan" and a "conditionally repayable contribution," the taxpayer failed to recognize that subsection 127(9) captures the economic substance of public financial aid regardless of whether the instrument is styled as a loan, contribution, or royalty advance.
2.2 Evidentiary and Contractual Failure: Inability to Satisfy the CCLC Technologies Commerciality Standard

Immunovaccine further sought to avoid the established appellate test for government assistance articulated in Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc. (96 D.T.C. 6527 (FCA)), The Queen v. Consumers' Gas Company Ltd. (87 D.T.C. 5008 (FCA)), Ottawa Valley Power Co. v. M.N.R. ([1969] 2 Ex. C.R. 64, aff'd [1970] S.C.R. 941), and Radio Engineering Products Limited v. M.N.R. (73 D.T.C. 5071). At trial, Immunovaccine sought to distinguish CCLC Technologies on the basis that its obligation to repay remained even in the event of failure of the project, because repayment was to be made out of all of its gross revenues; on appeal, it did not dispute that the CCLC Technologies test has been adopted to determine whether a payment constitutes government assistance, but contended that it did not need to satisfy that test because it was in essence a "judge-made rule," urging the Court instead to apply the ejusdem generis rule to the text of subsection 127(9).

The Tax Court found the attempt to distinguish CCLC Technologies unconvincing, and the Federal Court of Appeal rejected the "judge-made rule" contention, both affirming that CCLC Technologies provides the authoritative legal standard for distinguishing a commercial business transaction from "government assistance" under subsection 127(9). Under this standard, the Court must examine the surrounding context and contractual terms to determine whether the public authority disbursed the funds "in exactly the same way for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private business, that is, for the purpose of advancing the interests of the payor". When the evidentiary record of the December 31, 2004 ACOA Agreement was scrutinized against this benchmark, five contractual features proved fatal to Immunovaccine's characterization of the funding as an ordinary commercial loan:

headers: Terms of the December 31, 2004 ACOA Agreement
Judicial Evaluation Under the CCLC Technologies Test

cells: Enabling Statutory Mandate of the Payor
Executed by ACOA pursuant to its statutory powers under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 41 (4th Supp.).
Demonstrated that the Crown acted in a public governance and regional economic development capacity to subsidize high-risk R&D, not as a private lender seeking commercial profit.
Contingent Repayment Trigger

Repayment was to be made by annual instalments calculated as a percentage of the taxpayer's Gross Revenues from the whole of its operations (2% where the preceding fiscal year's Gross Revenues were less than $5,000,000; 10% where they were $5,000,000 or greater), with the first repayment due on December 1, 2008 and subsequent repayments due annually until repaid in full.

Because the taxpayer had not commenced commercial operations, had little or no revenue, and depended on further financing when the Agreement was signed, it was only required to repay to the extent it earned gross revenues from any source, after a four-year respite and at a fairly moderate rate; total repayments for 2008 to 2011 ($36,973.24) amounted to less than one percent of the contribution, leaving the downside business risk with the public purse.
Termination Provisions and the 2017 Atlantic Canada Production Period

Schedule 1, section 7.1 provided that the Agreement terminates when all amounts due have been paid in full or the obligation is otherwise discharged to ACOA's satisfaction, or, notwithstanding that, where the Schedule 4 commercialization undertakings have been fulfilled and the taxpayer demonstrates that Gross Revenues have not been or will not continue to be generated; Schedule 4 required the resulting products to be exploited through production in Atlantic Canada until September 30, 2017.

The Tax Court did not rely on a sunset clause; the taxpayer argued that section 7.1(b) merely reflected business reality, while the Court focused on the revenue-contingent repayment terms and ACOA's public-policy objectives. On appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal listed among the provisions pointing to government assistance that the Agreement ends in 2017 whether or not there has been repayment (2014 FCA 196, para. 16).
Interest Rate and Return Ceiling

The contribution bore 0% interest, with interest at the Interest Rate payable only on overpayments, on default, or on overdue amounts (Schedule 1, sections 4.1, 8 and 10.3); the maximum ACOA could ever recover was the nominal return of its $3,786,474 principal contribution.

The Court held that ACOA could not receive any net profit on the money advanced, a best-case scenario comparable to CCLC Technologies, which, combined with ACOA's objectives under the ACOA Act, showed that ACOA was not dealing with the taxpayer on basic commercial terms; the taxpayer's evidence that zero-percent interest is realistic in automobile financing was qualified by its witness's admission that such loans are secured by the vehicles.
Administrative Reporting and Use Covenants

Imposed quarterly and annual progress reporting (Schedule 5), payment on itemized claims for Eligible Costs (Schedule 3), a possible 10% holdback pending audit, and an obligation to exploit the resulting products through production in Atlantic Canada (Schedule 4).

The Court held these obligations to be representative of what is required when money is disbursed in the public interest, emphasizing the performance of work in Atlantic Canada and job creation; ACOA's surveillance was consistent with the role of a prudent grant-giver assuring itself that its contribution was being spent as intended, and ACOA measured project success by criteria that did not include repayment.

body.text: 2.3 Project Scoping and Cost Segregation Failure Under Subsections 127(18) and 127(19)

A practical lesson that advisors may draw from Immunovaccine—although the Court itself did not address cost segregation, the sole issue before it being whether the ACOA contribution was "government assistance"—concerns how a taxpayer structures the scope of a contribution agreement relative to its broader R&D and commercialization budget. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA, as reflected in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, government assistance reduces the SR&ED expenditure pool and qualified expenditures only to the extent that the assistance is received or receivable "in respect of" SR&ED.

In biotechnology and pharmaceutical development, a corporation's multi-year product pipeline typically encompasses two distinct spheres of expenditure. The first sphere comprises core scientific research and experimental development satisfying the definition in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, such as resolving technological uncertainties regarding antigen stability, liposomal encapsulation, or immune response kinetics. The second sphere comprises non-SR&ED commercial, regulatory, and infrastructure activities excluded from subsection 248(1), such as Phase III clinical trials with predetermined protocols, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) commercial facility validation, market development, intellectual property patenting, and regulatory submissions.

When a taxpayer executes a blanket contribution agreement with an agency such as ACOA that defines the "Eligible Project Costs" to cover the exact same laboratory wages, materials, and subcontractor expenses claimed on Form T661 for SR&ED, subsection 127(18) requires a dollar-for-dollar reduction of the qualified SR&ED expenditures. Furthermore, where the assistance exceeds the recipient's own qualified expenditures, subsections 127(19) to 127(21) can apply the excess to reduce the qualified expenditures of non-arm's length persons that performed SR&ED while not dealing at arm's length with the recipient. In Immunovaccine's case, the Agreement provided for a contribution "in respect of the Project" (the New Peptide-based Vaccines Project) equal to the lesser of 51.825% of Eligible Costs (estimated at $7,306,297) or $3,786,474, payable on itemized claims, and once the Court held the contribution to be government assistance, the Minister's denial of the SR&ED claims and related RITCs for the taxation years ended March 31, 2005 through 2008 was confirmed; the Court made no finding on whether allocating the funding to non-SR&ED activities would have altered that result.
2.4 Accrual Accounting Mismatch and the Post-Immunovaccine / CAE Doctrinal Evolution

The Immunovaccine decision also exposes the severe timing asymmetry embedded in the ITA for conditionally repayable government contributions. Because paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) operate on an accrual basis—capturing any assistance that the taxpayer "has received, is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive" on or before the filing-due date—the full $3,786,474 reduced Immunovaccine's SR&ED pools immediately in the 2005–2008 taxation years. By contrast, relief for any subsequent repayments under paragraph 37(1)(c) and paragraph (e.1) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) is strictly deferred until the future taxation year in which cash repayment is actually made. For an early-stage CCPC relying on immediate 35% Refundable Investment Tax Credits under subsection 127.1(1) to finance ongoing laboratory burn, deferring ITC recovery until the contribution is actually repaid out of gross revenues—Immunovaccine's repayments began only in 2008 and totalled $36,973.24 through 2011, and, as its CFO testified, because it became a public company in 2009 it would receive a substantially lower credit even if it repaid ACOA (a consequence the Court held did not alter the interpretation of the Agreement)—permanently destroys a substantial portion of the tax incentive's net present value.

The doctrinal reach of Immunovaccine expanded even further in CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57 (per Ouimet J.), affirmed in CAE Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 178 (leave to appeal to SCC refused May 25, 2023). Relying directly on Immunovaccine and CCLC Technologies, the Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal held in CAE Inc. that even an unconditionally repayable, non-forgivable government loan under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) program constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9)—and was simultaneously taxable as income on receipt under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv)—because its concessional interest rate and long-term structure were not "strictly commercial" compared to private debt markets.

Recognizing that the combined effect of Immunovaccine and CAE Inc. threatened to penalize Canadian innovators accessing bona fide repayable public loans, the Department of Finance announced targeted legislative amendments in the November 21, 2023 Fall Economic Statement, enacted by the Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1, S.C. 2024, c. 17 (Royal Assent June 20, 2024), which added subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ix) and the definition "excluded loan" in subsection 12(11) and amended the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) to exclude an excluded loan, for loans made after December 31, 2019. Crucially, while these statutory amendments overrule the extreme extension of the doctrine to bona fide, unconditionally repayable zero- or low-interest government loans, they specifically require that the arrangement be a loan, other than a forgivable loan, evidenced in writing, for which bona fide arrangements were made at the time the loan was made for repayment within a reasonable time, and the funds from which were used for the purpose of earning income from a business or property. Consequently, an arrangement structured like Immunovaccine's 2004 ACOA Agreement—where repayment is owed only as a percentage of gross revenues actually earned, no interest is payable absent default, the payor can never recover more than its contribution, and the agreement may terminate under section 7.1(b) of Schedule 1 without full repayment if gross revenues are not generated—remains squarely exposed to characterization as "government assistance" unless proactively restructured.

The following table maps each statutory and common-law requirement examined in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. The Queen (2013 TCC 103) against the taxpayer's specific legal or evidentiary deficiency and the governing standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal.

Court's Standard of Proof and Judicial Test

cells: Scope of "Government Assistance" Definition

Subsection 127(9) of the ITA (as it read for the taxation years at issue): "assistance from a government, municipality or other public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance or as any other form of assistance other than as a deduction under subsection 127(5) or 127(6)".

Relied on the ejusdem generis rule to argue that "any other form of assistance" was confined to the genus of the enumerated items, whose common factor was said to be a transfer of funds with no expectation of repayment, and separately argued that the contribution was not a "forgivable loan" but a regular loan outside the definition.

Purposive and Expansive Statutory Construction: At para. 45 (aff'd 2014 FCA 196 at para. 15), the Court held that the enumerated terms attempt to describe all possible forms of assistance, that "government assistance" extends beyond purely gratuitous acts of government, and that a contribution that is made by the government and is repayable may constitute government assistance.
Commerciality vs. Public Governance Purpose

Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc. (96 DTC 6527 (FCA)); The Queen v. Consumers' Gas Co. (87 DTC 5008 (FCA)); Ottawa Valley Power Co. v. M.N.R. ([1969] 2 Ex. C.R. 64, aff'd [1970] SCR 941); Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 41 (4th Supp.).

At trial, sought to distinguish CCLC Technologies on the ground that its repayment obligation survived project failure because repayment was owed out of all gross revenues; on appeal, did not dispute that the CCLC Technologies test had been adopted, but argued it was an inapplicable "judge-made rule".

The Ordinary Business Relationship Test: To avoid classification as government assistance, the taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities that the public authority disbursed funds "in exactly the same way for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private business, that is, for the purpose of advancing the [business] interests of the payor".
Unconditional Debt Obligation vs. Contingent Forgiveness
Subsection 127(9) ("forgivable loan" / "other form of assistance"); Radio Engineering Products Ltd. v. M.N.R. (73 DTC 5071); CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, s. 4.2.1.

Executed an agreement where repayment was owed only as a percentage (2% or 10%) of future gross revenues beginning December 1, 2008, bearing 0% interest absent default, capping recovery at nominal principal, and terminable under section 7.1(b) of Schedule 1 without full repayment if gross revenues were not generated (the Federal Court of Appeal further read the Agreement as ending in 2017 whether or not repaid).

Substance Over Form in Debt Characterization: The Court held that whether the Agreement could be labelled a loan was not determinative; applying CCLC Technologies, a contribution under which the public authority cannot earn any net profit, is repaid only to the extent of gross revenues, and is advanced to carry out a legislative scheme of economic development is a contribution toward project costs (assistance), not a commercial loan.
Mandatory Reduction of Deductible SR&ED Pool and Qualified Expenditures
Paragraph 37(1)(d), paragraph (h) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), and subsection 127(18) of the ITA.

Claimed its SR&ED expenses and related RITCs for the 2005–2008 taxation years without reducing them for the $3,786,474 received from ACOA, on the position that the contribution was an ordinary loan rather than government assistance.

Strict Accrual Net-Cost Accounting: Any government assistance "received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received" on or before the filing-due date in respect of SR&ED must reduce the subsection 37(1) pool and subsection 127(18) qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar in the year.
Entitlement to Refundable Investment Tax Credits (RITCs)
Subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127.1(1), and paragraph 152(1)(b) of the ITA; Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33.

Claimed full RITCs under subsection 127.1(1) on gross SR&ED expenditures without accounting for the ACOA subsidy, and, on appeal, failed to demonstrate any palpable and overriding error in the Tax Court judge's findings of fact or of mixed fact and law, or any other reviewable error.

Net Qualified Expenditure Threshold: RITCs under subsection 127.1(1) may only be generated on positive net qualified expenditures remaining after deducting all paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) government assistance.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their tax advisors can proactively structure public-sector funding arrangements and R&D operations to avoid the disallowance traps established in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. The Queen (2013 TCC 103), the following two industry case studies detail step-by-step remedial architectures. Each case study integrates the judicial test from Immunovaccine and CCLC Technologies, the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, and the contemporary statutory framework of the ITA, including subsections 12(11), 37(1), 127(9), and 127(18) through 127(21).
4.1 Case Study 1: Atlantic Canadian Biotechnology Developer (Segregating Regional Development Funding and Restructuring Contingent Royalty Contributions)
Factual Scenario and Impending Legal Pitfall

Maritime BioTherapeutics Inc. ("MBI") is a Halifax-based Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) developing a thermostable mucosal RNA vaccine platform targeting respiratory pathogens. For its upcoming four-year fiscal cycle, MBI budgets $10,000,000 in total corporate outlays divided across two distinct operational areas. The first operational area encompasses $6,000,000 in core experimental development qualifying as SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, consisting of bench-scale lipid-nanoparticle (LNP) formulation synthesis, microfluidic shear-stress experimentation, and in vivo murine immunogenicity assays aimed at resolving fundamental technological uncertainties regarding mucosal mucociliary clearance. As a qualifying CCPC, MBI expects these $6,000,000 of current SR&ED expenditures to generate $2,100,000 in federal Refundable Investment Tax Credits at the 35% enhanced RITC rate under subsections 127(10.1) and 127.1(1), alongside provincial Nova Scotia R&D tax credits. The second operational area encompasses $4,000,000 in commercialization, regulatory, and facility scale-up expenditures that do not qualify as SR&ED under subsection 248(1), including the construction and validation of a Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) cleanroom fill-finish suite, global patent portfolio prosecution, regulatory dossier preparation for Health Canada, and commercial business development.

To bridge its financing gap, MBI negotiates a $4,000,000 funding package with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency (ACOA) under the Regional Economic Growth through Innovation (REGI) and Atlantic Innovation Fund framework. In the initial draft Contribution Agreement prepared by the agency's program officers, the Statement of Work broadly describes the funded project as the "Development and Commercialization of the Thermostable Mucosal Vaccine Platform" and lists MBI's research scientists' salaries, laboratory consumables, and animal testing subcontracts as the "Eligible Costs" reimbursed at 50% across the company's entire budget. Furthermore, the draft contract stipulates a 0% interest rate, repayments calculated at 5% of gross vaccine licensing revenues, and an automatic sunset clause extinguishing any unpaid balance 10 years after project completion.

If MBI executes this draft Agreement, the CRA will apply Immunovaccine (2013 TCC 103) to classify the entire $4,000,000 inflow as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) because ACOA is acting under its statutory development mandate and the contingent, revenue-linked, sunset-extinguishable terms fail both the CCLC Technologies commerciality test and the bona fide loan criteria under subsection 12(11). Worse still, because the Agreement's "Eligible Costs" directly reimburse MBI's SR&ED wages and laboratory materials, paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) will reduce MBI's $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures by up to $4,000,000, destroying up to $1,400,000 in immediate federal cash RITCs under subsection 127.1(1).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Project Governance and Cost-Center Segregation ("In Respect Of" Ring-Fencing)

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA, as interpreted in section 2.0 and section 4.3 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, government assistance reduces the SR&ED expenditure pool and qualified expenditures only if the assistance is received or receivable "in respect of" SR&ED expenditures. Assistance received specifically to fund non-SR&ED business activities, commercial infrastructure, or non-eligible clinical and regulatory milestones does not reduce the subsection 37(1) SR&ED pool or subsection 127(18) qualified expenditures.

Before executing the ACOA contract, MBI must restructure its internal corporate governance via a formal Board of Directors resolution establishing two legally and operationally distinct internal programs. The first internal program, designated as Program A (Experimental Immunogen Research — 100% Self-Funded SR&ED), must be governed by the Chief Scientific Officer and encompass exclusively bench-scale hypothesis testing and experimental LNP formulation under subsection 248(1). The second internal program, designated as Program B (GMP Biomanufacturing Scale-Up, Regulatory & Commercialization — ACOA-Funded Non-SR&ED), must be governed by the Vice President of Commercial Operations and encompass exclusively GMP cleanroom engineering, commercial fill-finish equipment acquisition, regulatory toxicology administration, and market entry.
Step 2: Contractual Redrafting (Dual-Pronged Realignment of Scope and Repayment Terms)

MBI's tax counsel must intervene prior to signing the ACOA Contribution Agreement to implement two decisive contractual modifications. First, counsel must revise the Agreement's Statement of Work (Schedule A) and Eligible Cost Breakdown (Schedule B) so that 100% of the $4,000,000 ACOA funding is contractually earmarked for, and reimbursed exclusively against, invoices and payroll from Program B covering non-SR&ED GMP facility validation, commercial manufacturing equipment, IP legal fees, and regulatory compliance. To reinforce this boundary, counsel should insert an explicit negative covenant in the Agreement stipulating that no funds advanced under the Agreement shall be claimed against, or applied to reimburse, Scientific Research and Experimental Development expenditures as defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA incurred under Program A.

Second, to the extent any portion of the public financing must touch Program A (SR&ED) expenditures, MBI must decouple that tranche into a separate loan instrument that satisfies the post-Immunovaccine and CAE statutory exception for bona fide public loans under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ix) and subsection 12(11) of the ITA. Specifically, the parties must remove all revenue-contingent royalty triggers and delete the 10-year sunset forgiveness clause. In their place, the loan agreement must establish an unconditional, binding obligation to repay 100% of the principal according to a fixed amortization schedule—such as 36 equal monthly principal instalments commencing in Year 4—backed by standard commercial default covenants, ensuring the instrument cannot be characterized as a "forgivable loan" or conditionally extinguishable subsidy under Immunovaccine.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation Alignment

To defend the boundary between Program A and Program B during a joint audit by a CRA SR&ED Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and a CRA Financial Reviewer, MBI must strictly segregate its contemporaneous technical documentation. MBI should draft its Form T661 narratives exclusively around the technological uncertainties of Program A, such as overcoming LNP aggregation during lyophilization above 4°C. Concurrently, MBI must ensure that zero technical objectives, milestones, or progress reports submitted to ACOA under Program B overlap with the experimental hypotheses documented in Program A's electronic laboratory notebooks (ELNs). All quarterly technical claim reports submitted to ACOA must verify commercial scale-up, GMP engineering validation, and regulatory milestones rather than experimental R&D investigations, eliminating any evidentiary basis for the Minister to allege that ACOA subsidized the SR&ED projects.
Step 4: Financial and Experimentation Tracking Architecture

MBI must implement strict general ledger and payroll segregation so that the CRA Financial Reviewer can trace every dollar of ACOA funding away from the Form T661 claim. In its enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, MBI must establish separate cost centers—specifically CC-100: Self-Funded SR&ED and CC-200: ACOA Non-SR&ED Commercialization—so that all vendor invoices submitted to ACOA for reimbursement carry CC-200 coding and are automatically excluded from the T661 materials and subcontractor schedules. Technical personnel who split time between bench R&D and GMP validation must record daily hours on bi-weekly timesheets mapped specifically to CC-100 (SR&ED) or CC-200 (Non-SR&ED), ensuring that only CC-100 wages enter the T661 salary calculation while ACOA reimbursement claims draw exclusively from CC-200 payroll registers. On its corporate T2 return, MBI will account for the $4,000,000 ACOA assistance received under CC-200 by reducing the capital cost of the non-SR&ED GMP equipment under subsection 13(7.1) or offsetting non-SR&ED current commercialization expenses under paragraph 12(1)(x) (or electing under subsection 12(2.2)), leaving the $6,000,000 SR&ED expenditure pool under subsection 37(1) and the $2,100,000 RITC claim under subsection 127.1(1) completely intact.
4.2 Case Study 2: Multi-Entity Aerospace & Autonomous Avionics Group (Containing Intercompany Assistance and Structuring Commercial Debt vs. Repayable Contributions)
Factual Scenario and Impending Legal Pitfall

AeroQuantum Systems Corp. ("AQS Parent") is a Canadian aerospace engineering corporation based in Montreal, Quebec, with a wholly owned, non-arm's length R&D subsidiary, AeroQuantum Labs Inc. ("AQS Labs"), operating in Ottawa, Ontario. Together, the corporate group is executing a three-year, $25,000,000 technological development program to build a fault-tolerant quantum-inertial navigation system for GPS-denied flight environments. Within this budget, AQS Parent in Montreal incurs $10,000,000 of eligible SR&ED qualified expenditures focused on avionics airframe integration and real-time Kalman filter sensor-fusion algorithms, alongside $5,000,000 of non-SR&ED commercial certification and flight-simulator tooling costs. Simultaneously, AQS Labs in Ottawa incurs $10,000,000 of eligible SR&ED qualified expenditures under a collaborative intercompany research arrangement focused on cryogenic cold-atom interferometer physics and laser frequency stabilization.

To finance the initiative, AQS Parent applies for $15,000,000 in federal government funding under the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF). The proposed funding agreement is structured as a single hybrid contribution to AQS Parent featuring a 5-year grace period, a conditional repayment formula tied to consolidated gross revenue growth over an 8-year window, a cap at 1.0x nominal principal, and an automatic forgiveness of any uncollected balance at Year 13.

Under Immunovaccine (2013 TCC 103) and CAE Inc. (2021 TCC 57; aff'd 2022 FCA 178), the entire $15,000,000 contribution will be classified as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) because it is advanced pursuant to a public innovation mandate with conditional revenue-linked repayments and a Year 13 sunset extinguishment clause. Furthermore, because the $15,000,000 assistance received by AQS Parent exceeds AQS Parent's $10,000,000 of SR&ED qualified expenditures by $5,000,000, two severe statutory consequences follow. First, subsection 127(18) will wipe out 100% of AQS Parent's $10,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures, reducing them to nil. Second, under subsections 127(19), 127(20), and 127(21) of the ITA, if the non-arm's length group fails to properly allocate the excess $5,000,000 of assistance—or if the assistance applies broadly across the joint R&D project—the CRA will apply the unallocated excess assistance to reduce the qualified SR&ED expenditures of the non-arm's length subsidiary (AQS Labs), while any excess assistance not applied to reduce SR&ED pools will trigger an immediate taxable income inclusion for AQS Parent under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Project Governance and Non-Arm's Length Entity Containment

To prevent the $15,000,000 public financing from contaminating both entities' SR&ED claims and triggering a subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) income inclusion, the corporate group must restructure project governance across legal entities before the funding agreement is finalized. The group should partition the master engineering program into two distinct technical charters. The first charter, the AQS Labs Charter (Cryogenic Quantum Sensor Core), must be executed solely by AQS Labs in Ottawa as an independent, self-funded pure-research project ($10,000,000 SR&ED) that is completely excluded from the scope, definition of "Project," and eligible expenditure schedules of the federal SIF agreement. The second charter, the AQS Parent Charter (Avionics Airframe Integration & Commercial Simulator Tooling), must be executed solely by AQS Parent in Montreal ($10,000,000 SR&ED plus $5,000,000 non-SR&ED commercial tooling), which serves as the sole contractual counterparty to the federal government.

In addition, to the extent any shared SR&ED project nexus exists between the non-arm's length corporations, AQS Parent and AQS Labs must execute and file prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) on or before the filing-due date of the transferor's tax return for the year pursuant to subsections 127(20) and 127(22). By formally allocating 100% of any residual SR&ED assistance strictly to AQS Parent on Form T1145, the corporate group prevents the automatic punitive default rules in subsection 127(21) from cascading unallocated assistance down to reduce AQS Labs' $10,000,000 qualified expenditures.
Step 2: Contractual Bifurcation and Commercial Debt Benchmarking

Rather than accepting a single $15,000,000 conditionally repayable contribution that fails the Immunovaccine test, AQS Parent's legal counsel must negotiate a bifurcated two-tranche financing structure with the federal agency, or co-finance with a commercial Crown financial institution such as the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) or Export Development Canada (EDC). Under Tranche 1, the parties limit the conditionally repayable contribution tranche to $5,000,000 and restrict its eligible cost schedule exclusively to AQS Parent's $5,000,000 of non-SR&ED commercial flight-simulator tooling and airframe certification costs. Because this $5,000,000 is not received "in respect of" SR&ED under paragraph 37(1)(d) or subsection 127(18), it reduces only the capital cost or deductible outlay of the non-SR&ED commercial tooling and leaves AQS Parent's SR&ED pool untouched.

Under Tranche 2, the parties structure the remaining $10,000,000—which finances AQS Parent's SR&ED integration work—as an unconditionally repayable term loan devoid of any forgiveness or revenue-contingency clauses. Specifically, the loan agreement eliminates the conditional gross-revenue royalty formula and the Year 13 sunset extinguishment clause—features that, like the gross-revenue-contingent repayment terms and the absence of any prospect of net profit for ACOA on which the Tax Court relied in Immunovaccine, point toward characterization as government assistance—substituting an unconditional, fixed 10-year principal repayment schedule with enforceable debt covenants and standard creditor remedies upon default. By ensuring that Tranche 2 satisfies all conditions of a bona fide repayable public loan under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ix) and subsection 12(11) of the ITA—or, if benchmarked under common law per CCLC Technologies, is advanced by a Crown financial institution on commercial interest and security terms matching AQS Parent's private-placement debt benchmark—Tranche 2 neither reduces SR&ED qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18) nor triggers an income inclusion under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv).
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Work-Package Isolation

To substantiate the structural separation before the CRA, AQS Parent and AQS Labs must implement rigorous technical documentation protocols within their engineering product lifecycle management (PLM) system using distinct Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) codes. WBS-1000 (AQS Labs — Cold-Atom Interferometer Physics) must be documented via independent technical reports, optical bench logs, and simulation datasets retained exclusively by AQS Labs. WBS-2000 (AQS Parent — Kalman Filter Sensor-Fusion SR&ED) must track the experimental avionics integration funded solely through Tranche 2 (the unconditional repayable loan) and internal corporate cash flow. Finally, WBS-3000 (AQS Parent — Commercial Flight-Simulator Tooling & Transport Canada Certification) must track the non-SR&ED commercial certification activities funded through Tranche 1 (the $5,000,000 conditional contribution), with all engineering compliance checklists explicitly segregated from the SR&ED claim files.
Step 4: Experimentation and Repayment Accounting Protocols (Recapturing Repayments Under Paragraph 37(1)(c) and Subsection 127(9))

In the event any minor portion of government assistance is ever determined to apply against AQS Parent's SR&ED expenditures, AQS Parent must establish a dedicated tax-accounting ledger to capture the statutory add-back upon repayment. Under paragraph 37(1)(c) and paragraph (e.1) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), read together with subsection 127(10.7), every dollar of government assistance subsequently repaid by AQS Parent that previously reduced qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) is re-characterized as a qualified expenditure in the taxation year of actual cash repayment. By maintaining a cumulative continuity schedule linking each original Notice of Assessment, the exact project-level reduction under subsection 127(18), and the annual wire-transfer receipts to the public authority, AQS Parent ensures that any principal repayments immediately regenerate deductible SR&ED pool room under paragraph 37(1)(c) and restore 15% (or 35%) federal ITCs on Schedule T2SCH31 in the taxation year paid.
4.3 Summary Comparison of Remedial Outcomes Across Both Case Studies

cells: Contractual Repayment Mechanics

Repayment owed only as a percentage of gross revenues; 0% interest absent default; recovery capped at the contribution; termination possible without full repayment if gross revenues are not generated (and, per the Federal Court of Appeal, an Agreement ending in 2017 whether or not repaid).
Unconditional fixed amortization schedule for R&D debt tranche (satisfying subsection 12(11) / subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ix)); conditional grant tranche isolated to non-SR&ED costs.
Allocation of Public Funds ("In Respect Of" Nexus)
Contribution paid in respect of the funded project's Eligible Costs (the lesser of 51.825% of Eligible Costs or $3,786,474) on the basis of itemized claims.
Ring-fenced by explicit contractual covenants and ERP cost centers (CC-200 / WBS-3000) exclusively to non-SR&ED commercialization, tooling, and GMP scale-up.
Multi-Entity Non-Arm's Length Spillover
Unallocated excess assistance cascades across related group members under subsections 127(19) and 127(21).
Contained via intercompany project partitioning and timely filing of prescribed Form T1145 under subsection 127(20).
Impact on Subsection 37(1) Pool & Subsection 127(18) QEs
Immediate dollar-for-dollar reduction of SR&ED expenditure pools and forfeiture of RITCs under subsection 127.1(1).
100% preservation of current SR&ED qualified expenditures and full retention of immediate Refundable and Non-Refundable Investment Tax Credits.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Advisors

The ruling in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. The Queen (2013 TCC 103; aff'd 2014 FCA 196) establishes an enduring principle in Canadian R&D tax law: the characterization of public-sector financing under subsection 127(9) of the ITA turns on substantive economic reality rather than contractual nomenclature. Whenever a federal, provincial, or municipal agency advances funds pursuant to a public economic-development mandate on terms that insulate the recipient from unconditional repayment—most notably through repayment calculated only as a percentage of gross revenues, zero-interest terms, a ceiling that denies the payor any net profit, and public-policy covenants such as regional production and job-creation reporting—the courts, as in Immunovaccine, will classify the inflow as "government assistance" under the expansive phrase "or as any other form of assistance". To preserve SR&ED expenditure pools under subsection 37(1) and maximize Refundable and Non-Refundable Investment Tax Credits under section 127, tax counsel and technical advisors must engage prior to contract execution, ring-fencing conditional contributions strictly to non-SR&ED commercialization outlays while structuring R&D-linked debt as unconditional, bona fide repayable loan facilities that comply with subsection 12(11) and the CCLC Technologies standard.
